title: Bēowulf
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 18–19, lines 456–498 (fitt VII). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t: Hrōðgār maþelode, helm Scyldinga:
sentences.l: Hrothgar spoke in speech-words, helm of the Scyldings:
sentences.i: Hrothgar spoke in formal words, protector of the Scyldings:
sentences.n: This is the same line as 371 in Fitt VI, where Hrōðgār first answers Wulfgār: ‘maþelode’ is the past of ‘maþelian’, the verb that introduces a formal speech, and ‘helm Scyldinga’ (‘helm’, a helmet, and so a protector; ‘Scyldinga’, genitive plural, ‘of the Scyldings’) is in apposition to the name. The colon opens a long speech, which Klaeber closes at 490 with ’. It answers the request that Bēowulf made at the end of Fitt VI (426–455), to be allowed to cleanse Heorot with his men; Bēowulf's last words there were ‘Gǣð ā wyrd swā hīo scel!’, ‘fate always goes as it must’.

sentences.t:
‘For [g]ewy[r]htum þū, wine mīn Bēowulf,
ond for ārstafum ūsic sōhtest.
sentences.l: ‘For deserts you, friend mine Beowulf, and for favors sought us out.
sentences.i: ‘It is for deeds deserved, my friend Beowulf, and for kindnesses, that you have sought us out.
sentences.n: The sentence is one clause with the verb last: ‘sōhtest’ is the second-person singular past of ‘sēcan’, ‘seek’, and ‘ūsic’ is an old accusative of ‘wē’, ‘us’ (it ends like ‘mec’ and ‘þec’, ‘me’ and ‘thee’). ‘For’ takes the dative, here two plural nouns, ‘gewyrhtum’ and ‘ārstafum’, ‘on account of’. ‘wine mīn Bēowulf’ is a vocative with the possessive after the noun: ‘my friend Beowulf’. ‘wine’ is the word used of Hrōðgār himself in ‘wine Scyldinga’ (Fitt II, 148 and 170) and in ‘wine Deniga’ (350, Fitt V); here he gives it to his guest. ‘ārstafum’ is ‘favors’ as in Fitt IV (317) and Fitt VI (382): ‘ār’ is favor, mercy, and ‘-stafum’ is a guess, ‘supports, acts’. The first words are damaged or emended, and the apparatus is long. Klaeber prints ‘For [g]ewy[r]htum’: the brackets mark the added letters g and r, and the italics mark ‘or’ in ‘For’ and ‘ew’ in ‘gewyrhtum’ as letters he changed. The apparatus gives the manuscript as ‘fere fyhtum’; I cannot tell whether ‘fere’ there is the Latin ‘almost’ (so that the manuscript is close to ‘fyhtum’) or the manuscript's own letters. Editors have read ‘Fore fylstum’ (‘for helps’), ‘Fore fyhtum’ (‘for fights’), ‘For werefyhtum’ (‘for man-fights’), ‘For wīgum’ and others; Trautmann and Chambers read ‘For gewyrhtum’, ‘for deserts’, from ‘gewyrht’, ‘deed, desert, merit’, which Klaeber follows. Whose deserts are meant is not said; the next sentences, about Bēowulf's father, suggest an old debt of kindness, but that is a guess.

sentences.t: Geslōh þīn fæder fǣhðe mǣste;
sentences.l: Struck your father a feud, the greatest;
sentences.i: Your father brought on the greatest of feuds by the blows he struck;
sentences.n: ‘Geslōh’ is the past of ‘geslēan’, which literally is ‘strike’ and in legal use ‘bring about by striking, win by fighting’; ‘fǣhðe’ is its object, ‘a feud’ (accusative singular), and ‘mǣste’ is the strong accusative singular feminine superlative of ‘micel’, ‘greatest’, agreeing with ‘fǣhðe’. ‘þīn fæder’ is Ecgþēow (263; the name is spelled ‘Ecgþēo’ at 373). The verb comes first, which puts the weight on the deed. The apparatus records that Holthausen, Schücking and Sedgefield put the subject first, ‘þīn fæder geslōh’, to mend the verse, and sends the reader to ‘T.C. § 17’, a section this transcription does not include, so the reason is not known here. A ‘fǣhð’ is the state of hostility that follows a killing, as the next clause shows: the blow that began it was a killing. The sense ‘brought on by his blows’ is a guess at ‘geslōh’.

sentences.t:
wearþ hē Heaþolāfe tō handbonan
mid Wilfingum;
sentences.l: became he to Heaþolāf a hand-slayer, among the Wilfings;
sentences.i: he became the slayer of Heaþolāf, by his own hand, among the Wilfings;
sentences.n: ‘Wearþ’ is the past of ‘weorþan’, ‘become’, and ‘tō handbonan’ is ‘to be a slayer’ with ‘tō’ and the dative: ‘Heaþolāfe’ is dative too, ‘to Heaþolāf’, so ‘he became Heaþolāf's slayer’. ‘handbona’ is ‘hand-slayer’, one who kills with his own hand. ‘hē’ is Ecgþēow. The text says nothing more of Heaþolāf here; ‘mid Wilfingum’, ‘among the Wilfings’ (dative plural, ‘mid’ taking the dative), places the killing in their land or company, and ‘Wylfingum’ at 471, spelled with y, is the same people, I take it, since the feud is the subject there too. Whether Heaþolāf was himself a Wilfing is not said.

sentences.t:
ðā hine Wedera cyn
for herebrōgan habban ne mihte.
sentences.l: when him the Weders' kin for army-terror could not have.
sentences.i: At that time his own people, the Weders, could not keep him, for dread of an army.
sentences.n: ‘ðā’ is ‘when, then’ and begins a clause: ‘hine’ (accusative, ‘him’) is the object of ‘habban’, ‘have, keep, hold’, which stands before ‘ne mihte’, ‘could not’ (past of ‘magan’, singular because ‘cyn’, ‘kin’, is a collective). ‘for herebrōgan’ is ‘for’ with the dative: ‘herebrōga’ is ‘army-terror’ (‘here’, army, host; ‘brōga’, terror), and ‘for’ gives the cause, ‘for fear of an army’; whose army is not said, though in a feud it is presumably the slain man's side. ‘Wedera cyn’ is ‘the kin of the Weders’, the Geats (glossary), and so Ecgþēow's own people; they cannot shelter him. Klaeber prints ‘Wede’ in italic because the manuscript has ‘gara’ (apparatus: ‘MS. gara; Gru., 4 Edd. Wedera’): Grundtvig and four more restored ‘Wedera’. ‘Gara cyn’ would be ‘kin of spears’, which does not fit a statement about Ecgþēow's own tribe, so the emendation is likely right, though the manuscript's meaning is not known.

sentences.t:
Þanon hē gesōhte Sūð-Dena folc
ofer ȳða gewealc, Ār-Scyldinga;
sentences.l: Thence he sought the South-Danes' folk over the waves' rolling, of the Ār-Scyldings;
sentences.i: From there he sought out the people of the South-Danes, the Ār-Scyldings, across the rolling of the waves;
sentences.n: ‘gesōhte’ is the past of ‘gesēcan’, ‘seek out’, and its object is ‘folc’, with two genitives hanging on it: ‘Sūð-Dena’, ‘of the South-Danes’, and ‘Ār-Scyldinga’, ‘of the Ār-Scyldings’, which names the same people again (variation). The Danes are named by compass-points elsewhere (‘West-Denum’ at 383 and ‘Ēast-Dena’ at 392, both in Fitt VI). ‘Ār-’ is probably ‘ār’, ‘honor, mercy’, so ‘Honor-Scyldings’; that is a guess, and I find the compound only here. ‘ofer ȳða gewealc’ is ‘over the rolling of waves’: ‘ȳð’ is a wave, and ‘gewealc’ a rolling or tossing (from ‘wealcan’, ‘to roll’), a plain way of saying ‘across the sea’. He comes as an exile, and the Geats' rejection explains the voyage. The semicolon ends this stage of the story.

sentences.l: when I first ruled the folk of the Danes and in youth held a spacious realm, hoard-stronghold of heroes;
sentences.i: When I first ruled the Danish people, and in my youth held a wide kingdom, a treasure-fortress of warriors,
sentences.n: ‘ðā’ is ‘when’. ‘wēold’ is the past of ‘wealdan’, ‘rule’, and takes the dative, ‘folce Deniga’, ‘the people of the Danes’; ‘furþum’ is ‘at first, newly’ (the same word is spelled ‘furðum’ at 323 in Fitt V, where it was rendered ‘just then’). ‘hēold ginne rīce’ is ‘held a wide kingdom’ (‘rīce’, accusative neuter) and ‘hordburh hæleþa’, ‘hoard-stronghold of heroes’ (‘burh’, fortified place; ‘hæleþa’, genitive plural), restates it. Two readings are emended. ‘Deniga’ has ‘ig’ in italic: the apparatus gives the manuscript as ‘deninga’, with a slash that I take to be a line-division, and Schücking prints ‘Deninga’; Thorkelin and three more print ‘Deniga’, which Klaeber follows (compare 1686). The sense is the same. ‘ginne’ has ‘nn’ in italic: the manuscript has ‘gim merice’, which Schücking reads ‘gimme rīce’ (‘jewel-kingdom’), Chambers ‘gimmerīce’, Sedgefield ‘gumena rīce’ (‘kingdom of men’); the editor Klaeber cites as E.Sc. (not identified here), Thorkelin (in brackets in the apparatus) and Holthausen read ‘ginne rīce’, as in ‘Genesis’ 230, where ‘ginn’ means ‘wide’; Klaeber follows them. The clause is a long subordinate beginning, and the main point comes at the next semicolon.

sentences.l: then was Heregār dead, my elder kinsman, un-living, a child of Healfdene;
sentences.i: At that time Heregār was dead, my elder kinsman, no longer living, a son of Healfdene;
sentences.n: ‘ðā wæs … dēad’ is ‘then was … dead’, a main clause after the ‘ðā’-clause of the last unit, so it says what the situation was when Hrōðgār began to rule. ‘yldra’ is the comparative of ‘eald’, ‘older’, and ‘mǣg’ is ‘kinsman’, a general word for any relative; ‘bearn Healfdenes’ (‘bearn’, ‘child’; ‘Healfdenes’, genitive) says which: Healfdene is Hrōðgār's own father (glossary), so Heregār is his elder brother. ‘unlifigende’ is a present participle with the negative prefix, ‘not living’, which says ‘dead’ a second time; the poem likes doubled statements. The text does not say Heregār reigned, but the placing of his death beside Hrōðgār's accession suggests it.

sentences.t: sē wæs betera ðonne ic!
sentences.l: he was better than I!
sentences.i: He was a better man than I!
sentences.n: ‘betera’ is the comparative of ‘gōd’, and ‘ðonne’ is ‘than’ after a comparative (the same spelling as ‘then’ and ‘when’). ‘sē’ is the demonstrative ‘that one’, used as ‘he’. The exclamation mark is Klaeber's. After the plain recital of dates and facts, the king breaks off to praise his brother and, by the comparison, to put himself below him.

sentences.t: Siððan þā fǣhðe fēo þingode;
sentences.l: Afterwards the feud with property I settled;
sentences.i: Afterwards I settled that feud with money;
sentences.n: ‘þingode’ is the past of ‘þingian’, ‘to make terms, settle’, and takes ‘þā fǣhðe’ as its object; ‘fēo’ is a dative of means, ‘with property’ (‘fēoh’ is cattle, then money; the ancestor of ‘fee’). The subject is not stated, and ‘þingode’ is the same form for ‘I’ and ‘he’; ‘ic’ follows in the next clause, so I take it to be Hrōðgār. A feud could be ended by paying a price for the dead man (the ‘wergild’, ‘man-price’, in other sources), which is what the next lines describe. ‘Siððan’ is ‘afterwards, since’.

sentences.t:
sende ic Wylfingum ofer wæteres hrycg
ealde mādmas;
sentences.l: I sent to the Wylfings, over the water's ridge, old treasures;
sentences.i: I sent the Wylfings old treasures, over the back of the sea;
sentences.n: The verb ‘sende’ comes first and the subject ‘ic’ after it, a common order for a new clause. ‘Wylfingum’ is the dative, ‘to the Wylfings’, with ‘ealde mādmas’ as the accusative object. ‘ofer wæteres hrycg’ is ‘over the water's back’; ‘hrycg’ is ‘back, ridge’ (‘ridge’ is the same word), and the waves are seen as a ridge. It is a short sea-kenning, a plain one. That the treasures are ‘old’ may mark them as heirlooms, which is a guess; it may only praise them. The people are called ‘Wilfingum’ with an i at 461.

sentences.t: hē mē āþas swōr.
sentences.l: he to me oaths swore.
sentences.i: and he swore oaths to me.
sentences.n: ‘āþas’ is the accusative plural of ‘āð’, ‘oath’, and ‘swōr’ the past of ‘swerian’, ‘swear’; ‘mē’ is the dative, ‘to me’. The ‘hē’ is not named. The only ‘hē’ since 459 is Ecgþēow, so I take it to be him, swearing to Hrōðgār in return for the payment; but the Wylfings' leader is not ruled out by the grammar. What the oaths were is not said; they presumably bound him to Hrōðgār.

sentences.t:
Sorh is mē tō secgan on sefan mīnum
gumena ǣngum, hwæt mē Grendel hafað
hȳnðo on Heorote mid his heteþancum,
fǣrnīða gefremed;
sentences.l: Sorrow it is to me to say, in my mind, to any of men, what Grendel has for me of humiliations in Heorot, with his hate-thoughts, of sudden-malices wrought;
sentences.i: It grieves me to tell any man, in my heart, what humiliations Grendel has worked on me in Heorot with his hate-filled schemes, his sudden acts of malice;
sentences.n: The sentence has an impersonal opening, ‘Sorh is mē tō secgan’, ‘it is sorrow to me to say’, and an indirect question after it: ‘hwæt’ is ‘what’, ‘hafað … gefremed’ is the perfect, ‘has done’, and ‘hȳnðo’ is its object, ‘humiliations’ (plural), with ‘fǣrnīða’ (genitive plural) completing it. ‘gumena ǣngum’ is ‘to any of men’, a dative singular with a partitive genitive. ‘mid his heteþancum’ is ‘with his hate-thoughts’, a dative plural of means (‘hete’, hatred; ‘þanc’, thought). ‘fǣrnīð’ is ‘fǣr-’ plus ‘nīð’, ‘enmity, malice’; ‘fǣr-’ may be ‘sudden’ or ‘dire’, so ‘sudden-malice’ is a guess. ‘on sefan mīnum’, ‘in my mind’, could go with ‘sorh’ (grief in the mind) or with ‘secgan’ (say it from the heart); the word order allows either. The emendation is ‘secgan’, where Klaeber prints ‘an’ in italic: the apparatus gives the manuscript as ‘secganne’, the inflected infinitive after ‘tō’; Sievers, Holthausen, Schücking and Sedgefield print the shorter form, and Klaeber refers the reader to his ‘T.C. § 12’, which this transcription does not include, so the reason is not known here; it was probably the metre. Hrōðgār speaks of it as a private grief.

sentences.t:
is mīn fletwerod,
wīghēap gewanod;
sentences.l: is my floor-troop, war-heap, diminished;
sentences.i: My hall-troop is thinned, my war-band;
sentences.n: ‘gewanod’ is the participle of ‘gewanian’, ‘to make less’, so ‘is … gewanod’ is a passive, ‘is diminished’. The verb comes first, and the two subjects are in apposition: ‘fletwerod’ is ‘floor-troop’ (‘flet’, the floor of the hall, where the retainers sat and slept; ‘werod’, a band, also spelled ‘wered’) and ‘wīghēap’ is ‘war-heap’, a band of fighting men. Both name the same body of warriors. ‘mīn’ is nominative, ‘my’.

sentences.t:
hīe wyrd forswēop
on Grendles gryre.
sentences.l: them fate swept away in Grendel's terror.
sentences.i: fate swept them away, in Grendel's terror.
sentences.n: ‘hīe’ is the accusative plural, ‘them’, put first, and ‘wyrd’ is the subject (fate, as in ‘Gǣð ā wyrd swā hīo scel’ at 455); ‘forswēop’ is the past of ‘forswāpan’, ‘sweep away’. ‘on Grendles gryre’ takes the accusative, ‘gryre’, ‘terror’, and ‘on’ may mean ‘in’ or ‘into’; I read ‘in the terror of Grendel’. The sentence puts the blame on fate and not on the men.

sentences.t:
God ēaþe mæg
þone dolsceaðan dǣda getwǣfan!
sentences.l: God easily can that mad-ravager from deeds part!
sentences.i: God can easily stop that reckless ravager from his deeds!
sentences.n: ‘mæg’ is the present of ‘magan’, ‘can’, with the infinitive ‘getwǣfan’ at the end; ‘getwǣfan’ is ‘to part, separate’, and takes a genitive for what is taken away, ‘dǣda’ (genitive plural, ‘from deeds’). ‘ēaþe’ is ‘easily’. ‘dolsceaðan’ is accusative singular of a compound, ‘dol’ (foolish, rash) and ‘sceaða’ (a ravager, an enemy that does harm); ‘dol’ may mean foolish, rash or mad, and ‘mad-ravager’ in ‘l’ is a guess among these. After the speech has told of losses, here he says there is a remedy, and he gives the work to God.

sentences.t:
Ful oft gebēotedon bēore druncne
ofer ealowǣge ōretmecgas,
þæt hīe in bēorsele bīdan woldon
Grendles gūþe mid gryrum ecga.
sentences.l: Very often vowed, drunk with beer, over the ale-flagon, warriors, that they in the beer-hall would await Grendel's war with the terrors of blades.
sentences.i: Very often, drunk with beer over the ale-cup, warriors vowed that they would wait in the beer-hall for Grendel's onslaught with the dread of their sword-edges.
sentences.n: ‘gebēotedon’ is the past plural of ‘gebēotian’, ‘to vow, boast’, from ‘bēot’, the formal vow a warrior made at the feast, to be kept in battle. The subject ‘ōretmecgas’ (‘battle-men’, Fitt V 332) comes after the verb and its phrases: ‘bēore druncne’, ‘drunk with beer’ (‘bēore’ dative of cause; ‘druncne’ nominative plural), and ‘ofer ealowǣge’, ‘over the ale-flagon’ (‘wǣge’ is a drinking vessel; ‘ealowǣge’ appears again at 495). The vow is in a ‘þæt’-clause with ‘woldon’, ‘would’: ‘bīdan’, ‘wait for, await’, takes ‘Grendles gūþe’ (‘gūþ’, battle), and ‘mid gryrum ecga’ is ‘with the terrors of edges’, which I take to mean the terrible blades of the men themselves, though it might mean Grendel's own deadly edge. ‘Ful oft’ is ‘very often’. Bēowulf has made his own vow in Fitt VI.

sentences.t:
Ðonne wæs þēos medoheal on morgentīd,
drihtsele drēorfāh, þonne dæg līxte,
eal bencþelu blōde bestȳmed,
heall heorudrēore;
sentences.l: Then was this mead-hall in the morning-time, lord-hall gore-stained, when day shone, all bench-planks with blood bespattered, the hall with sword-gore;
sentences.i: Then, at morning, when day broke, this mead-hall was a lord's hall stained with gore, all the bench-boards spattered with blood, the hall itself with sword-gore;
sentences.n: ‘Ðonne’ is ‘then’, the ‘þonne’ in the next line is ‘when’; ‘þēos medoheal’ is ‘this mead-hall’ (‘þēos’ is the feminine nominative of ‘this’). The verb ‘wæs’ is stated once, for ‘þēos medoheal’; the later phrases, ‘eal bencþelu’ and ‘heall’, have none, and the reader supplies ‘was’. ‘drihtsele’ is ‘lord-hall’ (‘dryhten’, a lord), and ‘drēorfāh’ is ‘gore-stained’ (‘drēor’, gore, blood; ‘fāh’, stained). ‘þonne dæg līxte’ is ‘when day shone’, ‘līxte’ being the past of ‘līxan’, ‘shine’. ‘bencþelu’ is ‘bench-planks’ (‘þel’, plank); ‘bestȳmed’ is a participle of ‘bestȳman’, which the lexica gloss ‘wet, steam’; ‘bespattered’ is a guess. ‘heorudrēor’ is ‘sword-gore’ (‘heoru’, sword; ‘drēor’, gore), dative of means. The morning is the time of the sight: the hall is seen after the night.

sentences.t:
āhte ic holdra þȳ lǣs,
dēorre duguðe, þē þā dēað fornam.
sentences.l: I had of loyal ones the less, of dear troop, whom then death took away.
sentences.i: and so I had the fewer loyal men, of the dear company that death took from me.
sentences.n: ‘āhte’ is the past of ‘āgan’, ‘own, have’, and ‘holdra’ is a partitive genitive plural, ‘of loyal men’ (‘hold’, loyal, as in Fitt VI 376). ‘þȳ lǣs’ is the instrumental ‘þȳ’, ‘by that’, with ‘lǣs’, ‘less’: ‘so much the fewer’. ‘dēorre duguðe’ is a genitive or dative singular, ‘of the dear company’, in apposition to ‘holdra’ (‘duguð’, the body of tried retainers, as at 359 in Fitt V); ‘þē’ is the relative, ‘whom’, the object of ‘fornam’, referring to them. ‘fornam’ is the past of ‘forniman’, ‘take away’, with ‘dēað’ as subject and ‘þā’ ‘then’. Both verbs are past: the king is looking back on losses already suffered.

sentences.t:
Site nū tō symle ond onsǣl meoto,
sigehrēð secgum, swā þīn sefa hwette.’
sentences.l: Sit now to the feast and onsǣl meoto, victory-glory to men, as your mind may whet.’
sentences.i: Sit now at the feast and, in good time, give thought to victory-glory for the men, as your heart urges you.’
sentences.n: ‘Site’ is the imperative of ‘sittan’, ‘sit’; ‘tō symle’ is ‘to the feast’ (dative of ‘symbel’, the formal feast). ‘swā þīn sefa hwette’ is ‘as your mind may whet’, a subjunctive of ‘hwettan’, ‘whet, urge on’ (the form is the same in the present and the past subjunctive, so ‘may’ is one choice). The middle of the sentence is disputed, and I cannot give a settled reading. Klaeber prints ‘onsǣl meoto, sigehrēð secgum’; the manuscript has ‘on sæl meoto’ (apparatus), and the apparatus lists many other readings: Kemble ‘on sǣlum ete’ (‘ete’ perhaps ‘eat’, a guess), Thorkelin ‘onsǣl meodo sigehrēðer’, Grein ‘sigehrēðsecgum’ as one word, Dietrich the reading Klaeber prints, ‘onsǣl meoto, sigehrēð secgum’, Holthausen ‘on sǣlum weota sigehrēðgum secgum’ and, in another place, ‘on sǣl meota (imperative of ‘metian’) sighrēð secgum’, Schücking ‘on sǣl weota sigehrēð secgum’, Sedgefield ‘on sǣlum tēo’ (‘award’) and Bright ‘onsǣl mētto’. Several of these take ‘on sǣl’ as ‘in good time, in a happy hour’ (‘sǣl’, time, happiness), and ‘sigehrēð secgum’ as ‘victory-glory to the men’, but the verb ‘meoto’ is a guess: perhaps an imperative of ‘metian’, ‘measure out, consider’, perhaps a noun. My ‘i’ puts it as ‘give thought to victory-glory for the men’ and my ‘l’ leaves ‘onsǣl meoto’ in Old English. The closing mark ends Hrōðgār's speech. The invitation to the feast is the plain part: the welcome is given before the fight is spoken of.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs Gēatmæcgum geador ætsomne
on bēorsele benc gerȳmed;
sentences.l: Then was for the Geat-men together all-together in the beer-hall a bench cleared;
sentences.i: Then a bench was cleared for the Geats, all together, in the beer-hall;
sentences.n: ‘wæs … gerȳmed’ is a passive, ‘was made roomy, cleared’ (‘gerȳman’, from ‘rūm’, ‘room’); the subject is ‘benc’, a bench, singular. ‘Gēatmæcgum’ is a dative plural, ‘for the Geat-men’ (‘mecg’, man), and ‘geador ætsomne’ is two words for ‘together’ in a row. ‘Þā’ is ‘then’. The narrator returns here after the speech, and the whole of the Geats sit down at once.

sentences.t:
þǣr swīðferhþe sittan ēodon,
þrȳðum dealle.
sentences.l: There the strong-hearted went to sit, bold in strengths.
sentences.i: There the stout-hearted went to sit, proud in their strength.
sentences.n: ‘ēodon’ is the past plural of ‘gān’ (the verb ‘go’ in its preterite ‘ēode’); with the infinitive ‘sittan’ it means ‘went to sit’. ‘swīðferhþe’ is a nominative plural adjective, ‘strong-spirited’ (‘swīð’, strong; ‘ferhþ’, spirit, mind). ‘þrȳðum dealle’ is ‘bold in their strengths’; ‘þrȳðum’ is the dative plural of ‘þrȳþ’, ‘strength’, and ‘dealle’ is a nominative plural adjective that the lexica gloss ‘proud, bold’, a rare word. The two phrases describe the Geats.

sentences.t:
Þegn nytte behēold,
sē þe on handa bær hroden ealowǣge,
scencte scīr wered.
sentences.l: A thane observed his service, he who bore in hand an adorned ale-flagon, poured for the bright troop.
sentences.i: A thane did his office, he who carried in his hand a richly decorated ale-cup and poured for the bright company.
sentences.n: ‘behēold’ is the past of ‘behealdan’, ‘observe, keep to’, and ‘nytte’ is its object, ‘service, office’ (‘nytt’, use); a thane is attending to his duty. ‘sē þe … bær’ is a relative clause, ‘he who carried’, with ‘bær’ the past of ‘beran’, ‘bear’. ‘hroden’ is a participle of ‘hrēodan’, ‘adorn’, and agrees with ‘ealowǣge’ (‘ale-flagon’, accusative; see 481). ‘scencte’ is the past of ‘scencan’, ‘pour out, give to drink’, with ‘scīr wered’ (‘bright troop’, accusative; ‘wered’ is a spelling of ‘werod’) as the people served; ‘scīr’ is ‘bright’, and why the troop is bright is not said. The cup-bearer is a position at court, here held by an unnamed thane.

sentences.t:
Scop hwīlum sang
hādor on Heorote.
sentences.l: The scop at times sang clear in Heorot.
sentences.i: The poet sang at times, clearly, in Heorot.
sentences.n: ‘Scop’ is the court poet-singer (glossary: ‘scopes’, genitive). ‘hwīlum’ is ‘at times’, a dative plural used as an adverb. ‘hādor’ is a rare word, perhaps the same as the noun ‘haðor’, ‘brightness, clear sky’, of Fitt VI (414), spelled with ā; here it is apparently an adverb, ‘clearly, brightly’, or an adjective for the singing; the sense is a guess from that noun. The rendering ‘sang clearly’ keeps both possibilities open. The scene now is the whole hall at ease, before the next speech begins.

sentences.t:
Þǣr wæs hæleða drēam,
duguð unlȳtel Dena ond Wedera.
sentences.l: There was the heroes' joy, a not-little company of Danes and Weders.
sentences.i: There was the joy of heroes, a great company of Danes and Weders together.
sentences.n: ‘drēam’ is ‘joy, mirth’ (glossary), the subject of ‘wæs’, with ‘hæleða’ a genitive plural, ‘of heroes’; and ‘duguð’ restates the subject: ‘duguð unlȳtel’, ‘a not-little company’, ‘unlȳtel’ being ‘un-’ with ‘lȳtel’, ‘little’. The litotes ‘not little’ says ‘large’, a way of speaking the poem often uses. ‘Dena ond Wedera’ is a pair of genitive plurals, ‘of Danes and Weders’; the Weders are the Geats (glossary), so the two peoples fill the hall. The fitt ends on the hall at its best: the guests are seated, the cup goes round, the scop sings.
